title: Traps
text: The failures we hit more than once, or hit once at real cost, with what we did about them. Most are silent: the code runs, the checks pass, and the answer is wrong. They are grouped by the stage where they bite. The examples are R, because our code was R; the shapes carry over to any language (see languages.md).

title: Traps
text:
Fetching and running the archive

Running the archive in place. A deposited script that saves a figure to a bare relative path overwrote a file the deposit ships, so the working copy no longer matched the archive, and the checksum check passed only because it had run first. Run every deposited script in a scratch copy, never in the downloaded folder.
Write calls split across lines. A search for code that writes files misses a write.csv( whose file argument is on the next line. Join continued lines before searching.
Shipped intermediates. A script ran cleanly against the deposit as downloaded while the script that should have produced its input had failed; it was reading the deposited copy. One deposit went from “four of six scripts run” to “five of six fail” once its intermediates were removed. Run a second pass on a copy stripped to raw data and code (schemas/archive_run_status.md).
The archive that runs and writes nothing. One deposit had every write commented out, so it ran without error and left nothing to compare. A clean exit is not evidence of anything; check what the run produced.
Printing nothing. In R, source() prints nothing unless told to (print.eval = TRUE), so a harness that sources the deposited scripts records exit statuses correctly while capturing an empty log. We concluded that no archive values were recoverable from one paper until we turned printing on and recovered over a hundred. A deposit that builds a table object and comments out the print call can still be made to print it.
A single container file. When the deposit is one zip or RAR, the “no unlisted files” check runs on a folder holding one file and checks nothing. Unpack into a folder of its own and check the members against a second manifest.
A reason for skipping work that was never tested. We skipped one analysis because its package was “unmaintained”; it had been updated the day before, and installing it surfaced the paper’s only real reproducibility failure. Three other packages we had recorded as removed turned out to install and run. Test the reason before accepting it.

title: Traps
section: Software that changed underneath the code
text:
Software that changed underneath the code

Dispatch drift. A test function from one package, given a model fit from another, used to fall through to a classical test. A later version of the second package added the method it was looking for, and the identical line began returning a robust test: 17 of 18 cells in one table moved, with no error or warning. Nothing but comparison with the printed numbers catches this. Expect it wherever deposited code combines two packages.
A package that changes another package on load. Loading one package replaced fourteen functions in base R and stats, and broke an unrelated package’s estimator for the rest of the session. To find such a package, record every function in the loaded namespaces, attach the deposit’s packages one at a time, and see which attach changes something. Bisecting by the failure finds only the first culprit.
The random-number sampler. R 3.6.0 changed how sample() draws. Seeded code from before April 2019 needs RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding") to reproduce itself (rules/stochastic.md), and the setting has to be restored explicitly afterwards, since on.exit() does not reliably restore it when scripts are sourced in sequence.
Sort order. dplyr 1.1 sorts character keys in the C locale by default, which puts every capitalised word ahead of every lowercase one. Every value stayed correct and the rows moved, and a cell-by-cell comparison against the published table reported 172 of 717 cells wrong when none were. Pass the locale explicitly, or compare by key rather than by position.
Weights that quietly disappear. Refitting a weighted model from its own model.frame() drops the weights, which pairs weighted coefficients with unweighted standard errors; it moved one coefficient’s sign. Pass the weights explicitly.

title: Traps
text:
Writing the rewrite

A modern equivalent that is not equivalent. Replacing base R’s expand.grid() with tidyr’s expand_grid() transposed a grid, because the two vary their arguments in opposite orders. Every number still matched; only the figure was wrong, and it stayed wrong for months until someone laid the rendered figure beside the published one. Compare every figure by eye, as well as its numbers.
Factor order in a deposited data file. A treatment variable stored as a factor whose first level was a treatment arm, not the control, reversed the sign of every contrast taken without releveling. The standard errors looked normal, the script ran cleanly and deterministically, and only the comparison with the published numbers caught it. Set the reference level explicitly.
A column name that shadows an argument. A helper written mutate(outcome = outcome) on a table that already had an outcome column assigned the column to itself, so the labels were wrong while every cell was right, and a later filter silently dropped a whole experiment. Name arguments so they cannot collide with columns.
A script that skips its own work. An if (file.exists(out)) guard returns the committed output instead of recomputing it, so the run passes while the code may be broken (Stage 3).
An output file that exists is not a render that worked. A loop that checked for README.md passed on stale files after a column rename had broken three reports. Check the exit status.
Unseeded draws. A pipeline with an unseeded random draw gives a different answer on the second run, and nothing downstream means anything until it is fixed. Run everything twice and diff the outputs.

title: Traps
text:
Building the ground truth

The printed value read as a number. A CSV reader that guesses types turns “0.80” into 0.8 and “-0.00” into 0, and the precision needed for the comparison is gone. Force the column to text, and check that the file on disk still stores the string (rules/rounding.md).
Hand-typed comparison values. A typed number that agrees with a note looks exactly like a computed number that agrees with the data. One repository had a typed coverage count of 11 a few lines below code that would have said 3. Generate everything except the printed values.
Selecting a row by the number you expect. Filtering pipeline output for the value the page prints guarantees a match. Select by key.
Joins that match nothing. A join on a column that was missing for two of the studies left 72 of 130 rows unmatched, and the table read as if nothing were wrong. Route every join through one helper that checks keys are unique on both sides and the result is one-to-one.
Building from the pipeline instead of the article. A ground truth built from what the rewrite produces cannot see what the rewrite does not produce. One paper’s first ground truth had 40 rows, all matching, covering little more than a third of the paper. Start from the printed page.
“At least one row per float.” A figure with one checked value out of more than a hundred printed passed that test for months. Report coverage as a fraction for each float (schemas/float_coverage.md).
Rounding a value before comparing it. A value stored as 0.0115 rounds to 0.011, while the full-precision 0.01150090 rounds to the printed 0.012. Compare from full precision.

title: Traps
text:
Reading the published article

PDF text extraction. Text pulled from a PDF changes characters silently. In one paper = came out as 5 and the minus sign as 2, so a printed −1.5 arrived as 21.5. Multi-column regression tables were mis-aligned by a column, which produced a phantom erratum that survived two reviews. Check every quoted sentence and every transcribed cell against an image of the page, and read numbers printed on a figure by position rather than in reading order.
Numbers written as words. A sweep for digits misses “five successive elections” and “in all but one study”. Run a second pass for number words.
The preprint. A preprint’s numbers are not the published numbers. Transcribe from the published version.
Testing a document against the wrong materials. A corrigendum restated one paper’s original confidence intervals differently from the article’s appendix. We first wrote that up as an error in the corrigendum. It was not: the corrigendum had redrawn the original analysis from its own working files, whose inputs differed, and on those inputs it was right. Check a printed number under the conditions of the document that printed it.

title: Stage 5: Errata
text: Every error the earlier stages turn up is written up in one itemized errata note per paper, rendered to a PDF that sits at the top of the repository and, in our case, also on my website. The corrected values in it are computed by the code at the time the note is rendered, so if a package update ever moves a number, the errata move with it.

title: Stage 5: Errata
Stage 5: Errata
text:
The note
errata.qmd renders <paper_id>_errata.pdf and writes errata_entries.csv, one row per entry:
entry, class, source, form, title, location, published, corrected, note, claim_ids, corrected_values, values_in_spans

class says what kind of error it is: quantity, description, interpretation, definition, label, float, cross_reference, wording, spelling, typography, or bibliographic.
source says how we found it: pipeline (the rewrite computed a different value), reading (reading the article against itself, its appendix, and its code), reference_audit (checking every reference against Crossref), publisher_record (an earlier published correction), authors_archive (our own files outside the deposit), or proof (the proofs or accepted manuscript).
form is full (the published and corrected passages, quoted in full), brief (a one-line correction), or note (an explanation with no replacement text).
published and corrected quote the passage before and after, with the changed values marked; claim_ids ties each entry to rows in the ground truth and the claims file.

Each entry’s corrected values are computed from the rewrite’s output when the note renders. The build checks that every claim an entry names exists, that only quantity entries carry corrected values, that every corrected value appears in the corrected text, and that no entry “corrects” a claim the pipeline reproduces. One rule caught several mistakes of ours: a corrected value must never render identically to the published one at the printed precision, because then there is nothing to correct.
Entries are numbered by severity, with the errors that matter most first, and once a note is public its numbering only grows: new entries are added at the end, so that anyone citing “entry 3” keeps pointing at the same thing.
Every quotation in the note was checked against an image of the published page. Text extracted from a PDF can drop characters, merge columns, or mangle symbols, and an erratum that misquotes the article is itself an error.

title: Stage 5: Errata
text:
Whether a conclusion changes
The pipeline can tell you that a number is wrong. Whether that changes a conclusion of the paper is a judgment, and we left it to the authors. When an entry did change a conclusion, the note says so plainly at the top.

title: Stage 5: Errata
section: Which errors go to the journal
text:
Which errors go to the journal
Most of the errors we found were embarrassing but trivial, and the scientific contribution of each paper stands without them. Sending dozens of journals a correction for every typo and rounding slip would bury the editors and devalue corrections as a signal. We used three tiers:

Every error goes in the errata note, beside the maintained code, where anyone reading the repository will find it.
An error that changes the direction or implications of a finding a reader would rely on also goes to the journal as a corrigendum, whether or not the finding appears in the abstract. In our experience, errors that meet this bar are rare.
Retraction is for findings that can no longer be relied on at all.

When a corrigendum was warranted, we used it to correct the related errors in the same article as well. The reasoning behind the tiers is in rules/severity.md, and the disposition column in the ground truth records which tier each error landed in.

title: Stage 5: Errata
text:
Done when
errata.qmd renders without error, every corrected value is computed rather than typed, every quotation has been checked against the published page, the build’s checks pass, and every paper_internal row in the ground truth has a disposition.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text: The rewrite is new code that reproduces every table, figure, and number in the paper from the deposited data, on current software, written the way STYLE.md describes. It is the part of the project that keeps the paper usable: when a package changes next year, this is the code that gets updated.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
Shape
We wrote one script per table or figure, named for what it produces, with cleaning kept separate from analysis and shared functions in a single maintained/helpers.R. Every script writes to maintained/output/. Next to each figure we also save a CSV of every quantity it plots, because a figure file can’t be compared with anything, while a CSV of its points can. Tables are written both formatted and unrounded, so that later stages compare full-precision values rather than what a table package chose to print.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
Three rules we held to
No published number goes in. The rewrite computes everything from the deposited data. When a script seemed to need a number from the paper (a threshold, a sample size, a cut point), that was nearly always a sign that the computation upstream of it was missing. The one exception is a number that is itself a claim about the data, such as “fewer than 5 percent of respondents failed the attention check”, which a dedicated script checks rather than uses.
No script skips its own work. A script that checks whether its output already exists and returns early can pass every test while being broken. Ours always recompute.
Every “can’t be computed” is a claim to test. Several times a comment in the archive, or in an early draft of our own rewrite, said that some number couldn’t be reproduced from the deposit, and it turned out it could. We treated such comments as hypotheses, and checked them.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
Errors versus choices
The rewrite corrects unambiguous coding errors: a typo in a variable name, a wrong index, the wrong column, a covariate left out of a specification the paper describes. It does not revisit analysis decisions. If the paper used a particular estimator, specification, sample, or set of standard errors, the rewrite uses the same one, even where we would now choose differently. A choice we’d make differently today isn’t an error, and treating it as one would turn the errata into a second paper.
The line isn’t always sharp. One case that came up repeatedly: a regression silently dropped collinear covariates, so the model actually estimated differed from the one the paper describes. We counted that as an error, because the paper’s own description says what was intended. When we couldn’t tell which of two deposited values the authors meant, we wrote the finding up as a note for the authors to decide, rather than picking one.
Each correction the rewrite makes shows up in the ground truth as a row where the rewrite disagrees with the archive (match_rewrite = FALSE, locus archive), and in the errata in Stage 5. We were careful not to carry a typo forward into the new code just because the old code had it; the point is that the rewrite is right.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
Software changes
The rewrite uses current packages and the current random-number generator. When either moves a published number, the ground truth records it with the locus environment. A few of these surprised us. A function can keep its name and arguments while changing what it computes: one test function, given a regression fit from a newer package, quietly began using a different variance estimator, with no warning. Converting an old grid-building function to its modern equivalent transposed a grid, which showed up only when we laid the new figure beside the published one. We now compare every rendered figure with the published version by eye, in addition to comparing the numbers.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
The same answer twice
We ran run_all.R twice from fresh sessions, checked that both runs exited cleanly, and confirmed that the second run left the output folder byte-for-byte unchanged. PDFs embed a creation timestamp, so we blank it when writing figures; otherwise every run “changes” every figure. A pipeline that gives a different answer on the second run has an unseeded random draw or depends on something outside the repository, and both need fixing before the comparisons mean anything.

title: Stage 3: Maintained rewrite
text:
Done when
run_all.R runs from a clean session, every table and figure in the paper has a script that produces it, no published value is an input, and two runs in a row leave maintained/output/ unchanged.

title: Stage 1: Archive check
text:
In this stage we pinned down exactly what each deposit contains and found out whether its code still runs, before starting the rewrite.
It helped to keep two questions apart. Does the archive run? is answered here, by executing it. Does the archive reproduce the paper? is answered in Stage 2, by comparing what it produces with what the paper prints. The two come apart more often than you might expect: some of our archives ran cleanly and reproduced little, and others failed on the first line yet reproduced everything once that line was fixed.

title: Stage 1: Archive check
section: The manifest and the download script

title: Stage 1: Archive check
text:
Running the archive as shipped
We ran each deposited script in a scratch copy of the deposit (never in the downloaded folder itself) and recorded what happened in ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv:
pass, script, role, exit_status, outcome, stopped_at

pass is as_shipped (the deposit exactly as downloaded) or stripped (only the raw data and the code, with any intermediate files the deposit included removed). We ran both, because a deposit that includes its own intermediate files can make a script look fine when the script that should have produced those files is broken.
role is cleaning, analysis, or other. A helper file that is only ever sourced by other scripts gets no row, since it never runs on its own.
outcome is clean, error, timeout, or not_run. Scripts we couldn’t run at all (several needed Stata, which we didn’t have) still got rows, with not_run and the reason in stopped_at.

Where it mattered, we ran under the conditions of the paper’s day. R changed its default random-number sampler in version 3.6.0 (April 2019), so for older code we set RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding") when checking whether the archive reproduced its own published draws. The rewrite uses the current default, and any number that moves because of it is recorded as an environment difference (see Stage 2).

title: Stage 1: Archive check
text:
What the run writes
Before running, we searched the deposited code for anything that writes a file, joining lines first, since a write call split across two lines is easy to miss. After running, we compared every file’s modification time and checksum with the manifest and recorded what had changed in ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv:
pass, file, effect, matches_deposit
effect is added, overwritten, rebuilt, withheld (an intermediate removed for the stripped pass that nothing rebuilt), or deleted, and matches_deposit says whether a file the run rewrote came out identical to the deposited one. When a run overwrote a deposited output with something different, that told us something: either the deposited output came from different code than what was deposited, or the software had moved. Running in a scratch copy is what made this table possible, and it also kept the runs from quietly altering the deposit we were trying to document.

title: Stage 1: Archive check
text:
Diagnosing failures
When a script failed, we recorded why, and left the deposit as it was: the deposit is the published record, and its failures are part of what we were documenting. The causes we saw most often, roughly in order: a function removed or renamed in a package update; a package that no longer installs; an absolute path from the author’s computer; a file the authors never deposited; and a script that depends on an intermediate file no deposited script creates. We learned to treat a “deprecated function” warning as a hypothesis about the cause; several times it turned out not to be the real problem.

title: Stage 1: Archive check
text:
Done when
The manifest verifies, the download script stops on any mismatch, and every deposited script has a row in archive_run_status.csv for each pass.

title: ground_truth/published_claims.csv
text:
The extraction: one row per claim the article and its appendix make, numeric or not (Stage 4). Unlike the other tables, much of this one is transcribed by a person: the printed values and the classifications are read off the page. It is reviewed by hand, committed, and read by both the ground truth build and in_text_claims.R.
claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, comparison, expect, needs_block, notes

title: ground_truth/published_claims.csv
text:
Allowed values
claim_type







Value
Meaning




pipeline
A number the analysis produces: an estimate, a standard error, a p-value, a sample size.


descriptive
A claim about the results, often with no number: significance, direction, order, persistence.


definitional
A number that defines the design: the number of arms, a scale’s range, a wave’s date.


structural
A number about the document itself: “three experiments”, the number of rows in a table.


transcribed
A number quoted from another source, such as another study’s estimate.



comparison



Value
Meaning




==
The printed value is the quantity, at the printed precision. The default for every row with a value_paper.


<, <=, >, >=
The sentence states a bound (“less than 5 percent”).


approx
The sentence hedges the number (“about”, “roughly”). The hedge’s tolerance is set in rules/rounding.md.


NA
The row has no value_paper.



expect: NA (the usual case: the check compares values), range, derived, shape, or absent. The meanings are the verdicts of the same names in Stage 4. The column records what the claims script declares; the script, not this column, is what decides.

title: ground_truth/published_claims.csv
text:
Rules

needs_block is TRUE for every pipeline and descriptive claim, and for any definitional or structural claim the pipeline can actually reach. The claims script must print exactly the claims marked TRUE, no more and no fewer.
digits lives here and nowhere else. Both instruments read it from this file, so they cannot disagree about a claim’s precision. The build also checks that value_paper, formatted at digits, gives back the stored string, which catches a wrong precision that would otherwise pass on both sides.
value_paper is read as text. A CSV reader left to guess will turn “0.020” into 0.02.
claim_type is the boundary of what gets checked, and nothing downstream audits it. We compared the descriptive and definitional rows within each section by hand, because the same construction, classified two ways two paragraphs apart, once left one of a pair of identical errors uncaught.

title: ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv
text:
One row per printed value or claim checked against the code: every cell of every table, every plotted quantity we could count, and every pipeline and descriptive claim in the text (Stage 2). The table is built by ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R as the last step of run_all.R, and the only values typed into it are the printed ones.
paper_id, claim_id, location, claim_type, claim, value_paper, digits, value_script, match, value_rewrite, match_rewrite, holds, defect_locus, disposition, disposition_reason, notes
The rules for comparing a computed value with a printed one are in rules/rounding.md, and for values from random draws in rules/stochastic.md.

title: ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv
text:
Allowed values
claim_type: pipeline, descriptive, definitional, structural, transcribed, as in published_claims.md.
defect_locus







Value
Meaning




paper_internal
The printed text is wrong: the code produces one number and the page prints another.


archive
The deposited code is wrong, and the page printed what it produced.


environment
The software changed: the deposited code, run today, gives a different number than it did then.


rewrite
The rewrite is wrong. We fixed these, so none should remain.


upstream
The problem is in something the paper relied on, such as a dataset or an estimate it reused.


unresolved
We looked and could not tell.


NA
No defect.



disposition







Value
Meaning




corrected_here
An entry in this repository’s errata corrects it. Computed from errata_entries.csv, never typed.


corrected_by_journal
A published corrigendum or erratum corrects it.


documented_only
Recorded and deliberately not corrected: a value within simulation noise, or an archive bug the rewrite repairs that never reached the page.


not_corrected
Known, and left uncorrected for a stated reason.


NA
Nobody has decided yet.



How the dispositions map onto the decision about which errors go to a journal is in rules/severity.md.

title: ground_truth/<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv
text:
Rules the build enforces

The locus rule. A row where match, match_rewrite, or holds is FALSE must have a defect_locus. A row where every comparison passes must not, with one exception: a bug the deposited code has, the page printed, and the rewrite at first reproduced, which an erratum names. Such a row carries archive despite matching everywhere. A row with no verdict at all may or may not carry a locus. The locus is set where each row is built, never as a default for the whole table.
Disposition follows locus. Every row with a locus gets a disposition, or NA while undecided. The build stops on any paper_internal row whose disposition is NA; the other loci are reported as a count.
The printed values are the only typed values. value_script, value_rewrite, every verdict, and corrected_here come from code. A typed number that agrees with a note is indistinguishable from a computed number that agrees with the data, and only the second is evidence.
Built from the article first. The rows come from what the paper prints, joined to what the pipeline produces, so that a printed value with no pipeline counterpart shows up as a row with an empty value_rewrite rather than not at all.
Joins are checked in both directions. Every join asserts that its keys are unique on both sides and that the result is one-to-one, since a join that silently matches nothing looks the same as a table with nothing wrong.
Rows are never selected by their printed value. Filtering pipeline output for the number the page prints guarantees a match.

Reading it

It means the deposited code, run today, does not produce the file the authors deposited: either the deposited file came from different code than the code that was deposited, or the software has moved since. title: Which errors go to the journal
text: Active maintenance finds errors in bulk, and nearly all of them are trivial: a 2.9 that should have been a 3.0, panels of a figure in the wrong order, a misspelled name in a reference. The scientific contribution of the paper stands without the fix. A few are not trivial. This page describes how we decided which was which, and what we did with each.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
text:
Three tiers

Every error goes in the errata note, beside the maintained code, where anyone reading the repository will find it. The note is public, itemized, and computed from the code (see Stage 5).
An error that changes the direction or implications of a finding a reader would rely on also goes to the journal, as a corrigendum. In our experience these are rare.
Retraction is for findings that can no longer be relied on at all.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
text:
Why not send everything
Sending every author’s list of small corrections to every journal would bury the editors in notices that change nothing a reader would act on. A corrigendum is a signal that something important changed. Spent on typos and rounding slips, it stops being one. The errata note takes the volume, so that the journal notice can carry the weight.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
text:
Where the line comes from
Existing policies say a good deal about the line between correction and retraction and little about the line between a corrigendum and no notice at all. We borrowed from both ends. The Committee on Publication Ethics reserves retraction for articles whose findings and conclusions cannot be relied upon, whatever the cause. Some medical journals ask for only a correction, even for pervasive errors, when the errors do not change the direction or implications of the results. Our second tier takes that phrase and applies it one level down: an error that changes the direction or implications of a finding warrants a notice in the journal, and one that does not can live in the errata.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
section: The abstract is not the test
text:
The abstract is not the test
It is tempting to send a corrigendum only for errors that touch the abstract. We did not use that test. The first error we sent to a journal concerned a persistence claim: the paper said the effect of fact-checks on factual beliefs was still detectable more than two weeks later at half its original size, and the corrected estimate was about a third of the original and could not be distinguished from zero. The claim was not the paper’s central finding and was not in the abstract. The article made it three times in the main text, though, and the durability of fact-checking effects is a question readers of that literature care about. A reader could rely on it, so it went to the journal.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
section: When a corrigendum goes, related errors go with it
text:
When a corrigendum goes, related errors go with it
Once a corrigendum was warranted, we used it to correct the related errors in the same article too, so that the published record and the errata note do not disagree. Unrelated trivial errors stayed in the note.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
section: Errors an earlier correction already fixed
text:
Errors an earlier correction already fixed
Some errors had been corrected already, by a corrigendum published years before. Those are recorded with disposition = corrected_by_journal. Reading the article against the old corrigendum also turned up sentences that went on restating a finding the corrigendum had withdrawn. Each of those sentences is an erratum of its own, and they went into the note.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
text:
Who decides
Whether an error changes a conclusion is a judgment the pipeline cannot make. The agent drafted the errata and flagged the candidates; the author decided, and for anything sent to a journal the coauthors decided together. When an entry changes a conclusion, the errata note says so at the top.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: Which errors go to the journal
section: How the tiers appear in the data
text:
How the tiers appear in the data
The disposition column of the ground truth records what happened to each error (Stage 2):







disposition
Tier




corrected_here
Tier 1: an entry in this repository’s errata corrects it. Computed from the errata, never typed.


corrected_by_journal
Tier 2 (or an earlier correction): a published corrigendum or erratum corrects it.


documented_only
Recorded and deliberately not corrected, such as a value within simulation noise or an archive bug that never reached the page.


not_corrected
Known, and left uncorrected for a stated reason.



Every error in the printed text must have a disposition before the build passes, since an error nobody has decided about is unfinished.
crumbs: Which errors go to the journal

title: What counts as an erratum
text: An erratum is a statement printed in the article, its appendix, or its references that is wrong. The Stage 5 list of what that covers is long on purpose: wrong numbers, numbers rounded the wrong way, misdescriptions, bad labels, wrong cross-references, typos, and bad references all count, however small. Most of the work of applying the rule was in the cases at its edges, which this page collects.

title: What counts as an erratum
What counts as an erratum
text:
The gray area: collinear covariates
A regression with collinear covariates is rank-deficient, and the software drops a column to fit it. Which column it drops depends on column order and on the software version, so the printed estimate depends on an accident rather than on a decision anyone made. The paper’s own description of the model says what was intended, and the fitted model is not that model. We ruled that these count as errata and corrected them.

title: What counts as an erratum
section: When everything matches and the paper is still wrong
text:
When everything matches and the paper is still wrong
Agreement among the page, the archive, and the rewrite shows consistency, not correctness. A paper can print exactly what its code produced while the code has a bug, and a rewrite written against the archive can inherit the same bug. One paper summed vote shares across merged precincts instead of recomputing them, and every comparison matched. Reading the deposited code, rather than only running it, found that error and others like it. Such an error is still an erratum; in the ground truth it carries the locus archive even though every comparison reads TRUE.

title: What counts as an erratum
section: The text against its own tables
text:
The text against its own tables
When a sentence disagreed with the paper’s own table and our computation supported the table, we corrected the sentence. When we could not tell which of two deposited values the authors meant (two versions of a variable, say, each defensible), we did not pick one. We wrote the finding up as a note for the authors to decide.

title: What counts as an erratum
text:
Approximations
A number the text hedges (“about”, “roughly”, “nearly”, “on the order of”) is held to what the hedge could reasonably mean. A number the text states without a hedge is held to its printed digits, even when the true value is close. A sentence that says effects run “between 0.30 and 0.50 standard deviations”, about estimates of 0.283 and 0.522, is an erratum: both estimates fall outside the interval as written. The details, including how wide a hedge is allowed to be, are in rounding.md.

title: What counts as an erratum
text:
What we left out

Differences within simulation noise. A value from a random procedure that falls inside the distribution of that value over seeds is not an error. See stochastic.md.
Findings we could not judge. When we looked and could not tell whether the paper was wrong, the ground truth records defect_locus = unresolved and the errata say nothing. An erratum we were not sure of would itself be an error.
Defects the reader never sees. A bug in the deposited code that the rewrite repairs but that never reached a printed number is recorded in the ground truth (documented_only) and is not an erratum, because nothing on the page is wrong.

title: What counts as an erratum
text:
Who decides
The agent proposes and the author decides. Whether a discrepancy is an error or a choice, and whether a correction changes a conclusion, were the author’s calls in every case, and for any correction sent to a journal they were the coauthors’ calls too. For most papers these decisions took about a quarter of an hour; the hardest took a couple of hours each.

title: Session start
text:
Paste or point the agent to the following at the start of each working session, with the bracketed parts filled in.

You are helping me actively maintain the replication archive for one of my published papers: [citation], with its deposit at [deposit DOI], in the repository at [path].
Read these first:

The guide’s README, and the stage file for the stage we are working on today: [stage], in both stages/ and agent/.
rules/erratum.md, rules/rounding.md, rules/stochastic.md, rules/severity.md, and traps.md.
The schema in schemas/ for every table you will write or read today.
The repository’s STYLE.md, if it exists, and its notes from earlier sessions, if any.

Then tell me, in a few lines, the state of the repository: which stages are done according to each stage’s “Done when” list, what is failing, and what you propose to do in this session. Wait for my answer before changing anything.
Ground rules for every session:

Do not change, move, or delete anything in the downloaded deposit. Run deposited code only in a scratch copy.
Never type a computed value into a table. Only the values printed in the article are transcribed; everything else is generated by code in the repository.
Never use a published number as an input to the rewrite.
When a check fails, find out why before changing the check.
When you find a possible error in the paper, record the evidence and propose a classification. Whether it is an error, whether it changes a conclusion, and what to do about it are my decisions.
Report every number about the paper from a command you ran in this session.
Before ending the session, write down what you did, what is still failing, and what comes next, in the repository’s notes.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text: Source of truth: stages/05_errata.md. Schema: errata_entries.md. Rules: erratum.md, severity.md.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text:
Goal
One itemized errata note per paper, rendered to PDF, with every corrected value computed at render time, and a matching errata_entries.csv.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text:
Do

Draft an entry for every error the earlier stages found, and for errors found by reading the article against itself, its appendix, its code, its references (checked against Crossref), and any earlier correction.
For each entry, set class, source, and form; quote the published passage and write the corrected one, marking each changed span [[like this]]; write a note explaining what was wrong and what the correction rests on; and list the claim_ids it corrects.
Compute every corrected value from the rewrite’s output when errata.qmd renders.
Make the render check that: every claim id exists; only quantity entries carry corrected values, one per id; every corrected value appears in the corrected passage; no corrected value renders identically to the published one at the printed precision; and no entry corrects a claim the pipeline reproduces.
Check every quotation against an image of the published page.
Order the entries by severity, most serious first, and propose which entries, if any, change a conclusion and which meet the bar for a corrigendum.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text:
Do not

Include differences within simulation noise, findings you could not judge, or analysis choices.
Type a corrected value.
Quote from extracted PDF text without checking the page image.
Renumber entries once the note is public. Add new entries at the end.
Decide whether a conclusion changes, or whether anything goes to a journal.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text:
Stop and ask the author

Before finalizing the list of entries: the author decides which candidates are errors.
For every entry that might change a conclusion.
Before anything is sent to a journal or to coauthors.

title: Stage 5 for agents: errata
text:
Done when
errata.qmd renders without error, every corrected value is computed, every quotation has been checked against the published page, the render’s checks pass, and every paper_internal row in the ground truth has a disposition.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text: Source of truth: stages/03_rewrite.md. Rules: erratum.md. Style: the repository’s STYLE.md.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text:
Goal
New code, on current packages, that reproduces every table, figure, and number in the paper from the deposited data.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text:
Do

Write one script per table or figure, named for what it produces, with cleaning separate from analysis and shared functions in one helpers file. Follow STYLE.md.
Write everything to maintained/output/. Beside every figure, write a CSV of every quantity it plots. Beside every formatted table, write its values unrounded.
Keep the paper’s estimator, specification, sample, standard errors, and seed.
Correct unambiguous coding errors (a wrong variable, index, or column; a covariate the paper’s description says should or should not be there; a rank-deficient model that silently dropped a column). Record each correction for the ground truth and the errata.
Use the current random-number generator. Where it moves a published number, the ground truth records environment.
Compare every rendered figure with the published one by eye, in addition to its numbers.
Blank the timestamps in PDF output.
Run run_all.R twice from fresh sessions, check both exit statuses, and confirm the second run leaves maintained/output/ byte-identical.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text:
Do not

Use any published number as an input. If a script seems to need one, the computation upstream is missing.
Write a script that returns early because its output already exists.
Accept a comment saying a number “can’t be computed” from the deposit without trying.
Change an analysis choice because STYLE.md or current practice prefers another.
Carry a deposited bug into the rewrite because the archive has it.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text:
Stop and ask the author

When it is unclear whether a discrepancy is a coding error or an analysis choice.
When two deposited values are both defensible and the paper does not say which was meant.

title: Stage 3 for agents: maintained rewrite
text:
Done when
run_all.R runs from a clean session, every table and figure has a script that produces it, no published value is an input, and two runs in a row leave maintained/output/ unchanged.

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text: Source of truth: stages/01_archive_check.md. Schemas: original_manifest.md, archive_run_status.md, archive_overwrites.md.

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text:
Goal
A verified manifest of the deposit, a download script that stops on any discrepancy, and a record of what happens when the deposited code runs.

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text:
Do

Build original_manifest.csv from the archive’s API, not by hand, with every checksum the archive publishes and every file’s byte size. For Dataverse, request each file in its original format.
Write download_original.R to download every listed file into original/, stop on any size or served-checksum mismatch, print any published-checksum mismatch, stop on any file in original/ the manifest does not list (hidden files included), and unpack any zip or RAR into its own folder checked against a second manifest.
Make it the first step of run_all.R, and run it.
Before running any deposited code, search it for every call that writes a file, after joining continued lines.
Copy the deposit to a scratch folder and run each deposited script there, twice: once as shipped, and once with every intermediate file the deposit ships removed. Run under the software of the paper’s day where it matters (for R code from before April 2019 that draws with sample(), RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding")). Capture printed output: in R, source with print.eval = TRUE.
Write one row per script per pass to ground_truth/archive_run_status.csv, including not_run rows with the reason for anything you could not run.
After each pass, compare every file with the manifest and write what was added, overwritten, rebuilt, withheld, or deleted to ground_truth/archive_overwrites.csv.

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text:
Do not

Run deposited code in original/, or edit any deposited file.
Fix the deposited code. Record why each failure happened; the failures are part of the record.
Treat a clean exit as reproduction. Whether the archive reproduces the paper is decided in Stage 2.
Accept a deprecation warning, or a recorded “package removed”, as the cause of a failure without testing it.

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text:
Stop and ask the author

When the published and served checksums disagree for a file that is not a converted tabular file.
When a script needs software you cannot run (Stata, a licensed dataset).

title: Stage 1 for agents: archive check
text:
Done when
The manifest verifies, the download script stops on any mismatch, and every deposited script has a row in archive_run_status.csv for each pass.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
In 2021, Limor Peer, Lilla Orr, and I proposed that researchers “actively maintain” their replication archives, updating the code as the software around it changes, so that published results stay reproducible for years rather than months (Peer, Orr, and Coppock 2021, PS: Political Science & Politics). For a long time, none of us did it, because it was a lot of work. With AI coding agents the work became cheap enough that I went back and did it for my published books and articles. This repository records how we did it, in enough detail that you could do the same for your own papers.
The guide is written for people. Each stage also has a companion file in agent/ that says the same thing as instructions a coding agent can follow. If the two ever disagree, the version written for people is the one we meant.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
Active maintenance: a guide
text:
The stages



Stage
What happens
What it produces




0. Setup and style
Gather the paper and anything else that can settle a question about it; set up the repository; write down how you like your code written.
STYLE.md, the published PDFs, the repository skeleton


1. Archive check
Fetch and verify the deposit, and run it as it was shipped.
original_manifest.csv, download_original.R, archive_run_status.csv, archive_overwrites.csv


2. Ground truth
List every number the paper prints, and compare each with the archive and the rewrite.
<paper_id>_ground_truth.csv, float_coverage.csv


3. Maintained rewrite
Rewrite the code, one script per table or figure, on current packages.
maintained/, maintained/output/


4. Claims
Extract every claim in the text, numeric or not, and check each one a second way.
published_claims.csv, in_text_claims.R


5. Errata
Write up each error with a computed correction, and decide which, if any, belong in a journal notice.
errata.qmd, <paper_id>_errata.pdf, errata_entries.csv


6. Report and publish
Render the README, publish and archive the repository, link the deposit to it, and schedule the check.
README.qmd, a DOI, a scheduled check



The archive check and the ground truth come before the rewrite because the rewrite is judged against them. The ground truth also starts from the article rather than from the code, for a reason Stage 2 explains: a number the pipeline never computes would otherwise never be compared with anything.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
What it cost
Our papers ranged from two-page research notes to a book, and the cost varied with them:

Agent time. Most of the work is done by the agent. A typical paper took a handful of working sessions spread over a few days; a long paper with a large appendix took several times that.
My time. For most papers, about 15 minutes to read the errata and decide what to do about them. For the hardest few, about two hours each, mostly spent weighing how serious an error was and digging up old files that could explain it.
Compute. Most pipelines run in a few minutes. Our slowest, a large simulation study, takes most of a day on a laptop.

The early papers took far longer than the later ones, because we were working out the procedure as we went. With the procedure written down, a new paper should go faster.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
What it found
Errors turned out to be common. A small share of all the claims our papers print were wrong, but most of the papers printed at least one wrong number, and nearly all of them had a mistake of some kind once typos and reference errors are counted. Most errors were small: a number in the text left over from an earlier draft, a value rounded the wrong way, two panels of a figure in the wrong order. Errors that change a conclusion were rare, and when we found one we sent a corrigendum to the journal. If your experience is like ours, you will find errors too.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
Languages other than R
Our papers were written in R, so the templates and examples are in R. The stages, the table formats, the checks, and the rules for judging errors are not tied to R, and languages.md lists the Stata and Python counterparts of the R tools we used. Stage 4 describes how each claim gets its verdict; the R package excheckr implements those rules, and nothing stops anyone from implementing them in another language.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
What is in this repository

stages/: one file per stage, with its purpose, inputs, outputs, checks, and the judgment calls it involves.
schemas/: the columns and allowed values of every table the procedure produces.
rules/: the judgments that kept coming up (what counts as an erratum, rounding, simulation noise, and when an error needs a journal notice).
templates/: starting files for a new repository.
agent/: the stages as instructions for a coding agent.
traps.md: problems we ran into more than once, and how we got around them.
languages.md: Stata and Python counterparts of the R tools.
examples/: finished repositories from our collection, and an example STYLE.md.

title: Active maintenance: a guide
text:
License
CC0. Take whatever is useful.

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text: Source of truth: stages/00_setup.md.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text:
Goal
A repository skeleton, the published record in hand, the deposit identified, and an approved STYLE.md.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text:
Do

Collect the publisher’s rendered PDFs: the article (version of record), the online appendix, and any published corrigendum. Do not use a preprint or accepted manuscript as a source of published values.
Find the replication deposit and record its DOI. Do not copy the data into the repository.
Ask the author which materials outside the deposit exist (production .tex or .docx, proofs, accepted manuscript, old working scripts) and where they are. Treat a working-folder .tex as the published text only if its compiled PDF matches the publisher’s.
Create the repository with the layout in the stage file: run_all.R (or the language’s equivalent), download_original.R, maintained/, maintained/output/, ground_truth/, errata.qmd, README.qmd, a .gitignore that excludes original/, and a license.
Use paths relative to the repository root everywhere.
Read the recent code the author points you to, and draft STYLE.md: script organization, naming, data manipulation idioms, modeling defaults, figures (with a CSV of plotted values beside each), tables, and things to avoid. Quote examples from the author’s code.
Give the draft to the author and revise it until they approve it. Commit the approved version.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text:
Do not

Let STYLE.md override the paper’s own choices. The rewrite keeps the original estimator, specification, sample, standard errors, and seed whatever STYLE.md prefers. Say so in STYLE.md.
Use materials outside the deposit as inputs to the rewrite. They explain errors; they do not supply numbers.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text:
Stop and ask the author

When you cannot find the deposit, or find more than one version of it.
When a corrigendum or erratum exists and you are unsure which version of a passage is the one to check.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style
text:
Done when
The repository exists with its entry point and layout, the published PDFs are in hand, the deposit DOI is recorded, and an approved STYLE.md is committed.
crumbs: Stage 0 for agents: setup and style

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text: Source of truth: stages/02_ground_truth.md. Schemas: ground_truth.md, float_coverage.md. Rules: rounding.md, stochastic.md.

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text:
Goal
One generated table comparing every printed number with the archive’s value and the rewrite’s value, and a coverage table saying how much of each float it checks.

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text:
Do

List every table and figure from the article and appendix themselves, and write a row for each in float_coverage.csv.
Transcribe every printed value from images of the published pages, as strings, with their printed precision. Read multi-column tables from the rendered page, not from extracted text. Read numbers printed on a figure by position.
Write ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R, run last by run_all.R. It starts from the transcribed values and joins them to the archive’s values (from the Stage 1 runs) and the rewrite’s values (from maintained/output/, at full precision).
Compare at the printed precision, by formatting the computed value and comparing strings, after the normalizations in rules/rounding.md. Compare the archive at the coarser of the page’s precision and the precision the deposited code printed.
For values from random draws, first confirm that something draws at random. For unseeded values, compare against the distribution over many seeds, leave match_rewrite as NA, and record the verdict in holds.
On every row where a comparison fails, set defect_locus where the row is built, and propose a disposition. Compute corrected_here from errata_entries.csv.
Make the build stop if: a printed value has been read as a number; a failing row has no locus or a passing row has one (apart from the documented exception); a paper_internal row has no disposition; any join is not one-to-one; or a float is missing from float_coverage.csv.
Compute every count in float_coverage.csv.

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text:
Do not

Type any value except the printed ones.
Select a row by its printed value.
Read the printed values with automatic type guessing.
Count a float as covered because it has one row, or because it prints no numbers.
Set a default locus for the whole table.

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text:
Stop and ask the author

When the page, the archive, and the rewrite disagree and you cannot tell which is wrong (propose unresolved).
When a value is wrong in a way that may change a conclusion.

title: Stage 2 for agents: ground truth
text:
Done when
The build runs last in run_all.R and passes all of its checks.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text: Source of truth: stages/04_claims.md. Schema: published_claims.md. Verdict logic: languages.md.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text:
Goal
Every claim in the article and appendix, numeric or not, extracted, classified, and checked by code that quotes the sentence and recomputes it.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text:
Do

Extract every numeric token from the article and appendix, then sweep again for numbers written as words.
Read for claims with no number: significance, direction, order, persistence, and counts in words.
Classify each claim (pipeline, descriptive, definitional, structural, transcribed), store the printed value as text with its precision, and set comparison and needs_block. Write ground_truth/published_claims.csv.
Compare the descriptive and definitional classifications within each section, and make the same sentence construction get the same type.
Write maintained/in_text_claims.R with one block per claim with needs_block = TRUE. Each block quotes the sentence verbatim in a comment and recomputes the claim from maintained/output/ or the cleaned data.
Where a block declares range, derived, or shape, make the block’s code test the condition. For a hedged number, make the block test the half-step bound in rules/rounding.md, since the check does not.
Run the file on its own, and check that the printed claim ids are exactly the needs_block ids.
Reconcile with the ground truth: every claim in both must have the same printed value, precision, and type, and where both compute a value, they must agree.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text:
Do not

Read the ground truth from the claims script. The two checks must be independent.
Refit models in the claims script.
Declare a verdict a block has not tested.
Treat an unhedged approximation as hedged.
Invent a computation for a quantity nothing in the paper or deposit identifies.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text:
Stop and ask the author

When a claim with no number appears not to hold.
When the two instruments disagree and you cannot tell which is wrong.

title: Stage 4 for agents: claims
text:
Done when
Every claim is in published_claims.csv, every claim that needs a check has one, the printed count equals the declared count, the two instruments agree, and the summary line shows no failing verdicts.

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text: Source of truth: stages/06_publish.md.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text:
Goal
A README a stranger can follow, a public repository with a permanent DOI, a link from the original deposit, and a scheduled check.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text:
Do

Write README.qmd for someone arriving from the article: what the repository is, a table of verified DOIs (article, deposit, repository), how to run it, an overview of the paper, whether the archive runs, the errata, the ground truth and each float’s coverage, the two claim checks, the rewrite, and the software environment.
Compute every quantity in the README’s prose with inline code.
Run the whole pipeline once more and confirm it leaves no stray or changed files. Check file names against a case-sensitive file system.
Write .zenodo.json with the title, creators, license, and related identifiers: the article (isSupplementTo), the deposit (isDerivedFrom), and the repository URL, listed explicitly.
Prepare the line that links the deposit to the maintained version (the Zenodo concept DOI and the repository URL), for Dataverse’s Related Material field or the OSF project description.
Add the scheduled check workflow, and confirm it passes once.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text:
Do not

Write the history of the project into the README.
Copy the deposit into the repository.
Pin old package versions to make a failing check pass; update the rewrite instead.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text:
Stop and ask the author

Before making the repository public, creating a GitHub release, or publishing at Zenodo. Each is visible to others and hard to undo.
Before editing any deposit’s metadata. Deposits in a journal’s collection, or made by a coauthor, need their curators or owners.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish
text:
Done when
The README renders with every number computed, the repository is public, its Zenodo DOI resolves and appears in the README and the errata, the original deposit links to it, and the scheduled check has passed at least once.
crumbs: Stage 6 for agents: report and publish

title: Languages other than R
text:
Needs review. Our code was R, so the R column below is what we used, and the Stata and Python columns are not. We drafted them from each language’s documentation, not from running the procedure in it. If you work in Stata or Python and find something wrong or missing, please open an issue.
The procedure does not depend on R. What it needs from a language is a short list of capabilities: build paths from the project root, run everything from one entry point, fix the random-number generator, compute the paper’s standard errors, write unrounded output beside every table and figure, verify downloads by checksum, read printed values as text, and format a number at a given precision. This page maps each one.

title: Languages other than R
text:
Counterparts









Need
R (what we used)
Stata
Python




Paths from the project root
here::here(), anchored by here::i_am()
A global set once in the master do-file (global root "..."), with every path built from it; no cd inside scripts
pathlib.Path, anchored at the repository root (for example with pyprojroot)


One entry point that stops at the first failure
run_all.R, sourcing scripts in order
A master .do file calling each script with do; Stata stops on the first error unless told otherwise
run_all.py calling each step with subprocess.run(..., check=True), or a Makefile


Fixed package versions
renv lockfile
Ship the user-written commands in the repository and point sysdir set PLUS at them; set version at the top of the master file
A pinned lockfile (requirements.txt with exact versions, or uv.lock)


Seeds and the generator
set.seed(); RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding") to reproduce pre-3.6 draws
set seed; the generator depends on version (version 13 and earlier give the old KISS generator, later versions Mersenne Twister); set sortseed for ties
numpy.random.default_rng(seed), passed explicitly; the legacy np.random.seed() and the standard library’s random keep separate global states


Robust standard errors
estimatr::lm_robust(), HC2 by default

Two cautions about the table.
Default standard errors differ across languages. Stata’s robust is HC1, estimatr’s default is HC2, and statsmodels makes you choose. A rewrite in a different language from the original, or a port between packages in the same language, can move every standard error in a paper without anything being wrong in the code. Use the formatting function, not a rounding function. Whatever you use, test it on values that sit on a rounding boundary.

title: Languages other than R
text:
The claims check
Stage 4 describes the verdicts. Rewriting the check in another language means reproducing this behaviour; excheckr is one implementation of it, not the definition.
For each claim in published_claims.csv with needs_block = TRUE, a block in the claims script computes a value from the rewrite’s output and declares it with the claim’s id and, where the claim needs one, an expectation (range, derived, shape, or absent). The check looks up the claim’s printed value and precision in the extraction, and the corrected value from any errata entry whose claim_ids name it. It formats the computed value at the printed precision, normalizing a negative zero, and then takes the first verdict that applies:

The block produced no value: absent if it declared absent, otherwise MISSING. (A block that declares absent and then produces a value is an error in the script, not a verdict.)
The block declared range, derived, or shape: that verdict. The declaration is the block’s own statement that it has tested the condition, so the block’s code must do the testing.
The claim has no printed value: shape.
An erratum corrects the claim: STALE if the computed value agrees with the printed value (the pipeline reproduces what the erratum says is wrong), DRIFT if it agrees with neither the printed nor the corrected value, and corrected if it agrees with the corrected value.
The computed value agrees with the printed value at the printed precision: match.
The claim’s type is descriptive: hedged.
Otherwise: MISMATCH.

Each claim prints one line: CLAIM <claim_id> = <computed value> || [verdict] <label>. At the end the check prints a summary counting each verdict and stops with an error on any MISMATCH, STALE, DRIFT, or MISSING. Two counts are checked separately: the claims printed must be exactly the claims with needs_block = TRUE, and every claim that a quantity erratum names must score corrected.
excheckr also has an optional band for values from simulations: a failing value within a stated distance of its target scores MEDIUM and passes. Whether to carry that over depends on how your rewrite handles the cases in rules/stochastic.md.

title: Languages other than R
section: Traps specific to Stata and Python
text:
Traps specific to Stata and Python
These are well-known hazards of each language rather than things we hit ourselves; they belong in traps.md once someone has met them in practice.
Stata

sort is not stable: observations with tied keys come out in an order that depends on the sort seed. Code that relies on the order of ties (taking the first observation in a group, say) can give different answers from run to run. Use sort, stable or break the ties.
A missing numeric value is larger than every number, so if x > 5 includes missing values.
generate creates a 4-byte float by default, so x == 0.1 can be false for a variable assigned 0.1. Use double (or set type double) for anything compared or reported.
merge m:m does not do what its name suggests; it pairs observations by order within groups. Use joinby for a many-to-many join, and check _merge after every merge.
version changes behaviour well beyond the random-number generator. Set it once in the master file to the version the paper used for the archive check, and to the current version for the rewrite.

Python

pandas guesses column types on read, which turns “0.80” into 0.8 and can turn an identifier like “007” into 7. Read anything printed as text.
groupby drops groups whose key is missing unless told otherwise (dropna=False), and sorts groups by default.
statsmodels’ array interface (sm.OLS(y, X)) does not add an intercept, while its formula interface does.
Library defaults change between versions more often than in R or Stata. Pin every version, and expect dispatch drift of the kind described in traps.md.

title: Rounding
text: The rule in one sentence: a computed value matches a printed one when, formatted to the precision the page prints, it gives the same digits. Everything below is about applying that rule without fooling yourself in either direction.

title: Rounding
section: Keep the printed value as a string
text:
Keep the printed value as a string
A printed number carries its precision in its digits. “0.80” says two decimal places, “0.8” says one, and as floating-point numbers the two are identical. Once a printed value has been read in as a number, the comparison at printed precision can no longer be made, because the precision is gone.
We therefore stored every printed value as the string the page prints, in the extraction and in the committed ground truth, and compared strings: the computed value is formatted with the printed number of decimals (sprintf("%.2f", x) in R), and the two strings are compared after the clean-up below. A comparison by numeric tolerance fails in both directions. Too loose a tolerance passed a value that the row’s own note said disagreed; values sitting exactly on a rounding boundary were reported as mismatches when they were not.
The string is easy to lose by accident. A CSV reader that guesses column types will read a column of numeric-looking strings as numbers, turning “0.020” into 0.02 and “-0.00” into 0. We forced the column type to character everywhere the printed value is read, and checked that the file on disk still stores the string, since a script can carry the string internally and then write a number at the end.

title: Rounding
Rounding
text:
Rounding errors are errors
A value rounded the wrong way at the printed precision is an erratum. The text that prints 0.23 for a value of 0.2230 is wrong at the precision it chose, and so is a value truncated rather than rounded (0.699 printed for 0.6996). These errata are small, and most of them are hand-typed numbers in the body text, where nothing generated them from the code.
The computed side must be compared at full precision. If the rewrite stores a value already rounded (an R-squared kept as 0.0115) and that value is rounded again for comparison, the result can disagree with the page (0.011 against a printed 0.012) when the full-precision value (0.01150090) agrees. Every table in the rewrite is written unrounded beside its formatted version for this reason.

title: Rounding
text:
Hedged numbers
When the sentence itself hedges, we compared within half a step of the sentence’s own precision. We treated the following words as hedges: “approximately”, “about”, “roughly”, “around”, “nearly”, “close to”, “on the order of”.

“about 37” tolerates 36.5 to 37.5;
“about 40 percent” tolerates 35 to 45 percent.

A hedge needs that bound. Our first version of the rule simply returned no verdict for a hedged number, and it hid one paper’s largest error: an appendix said one effect was “about 37 percentage points” when the estimate was 29.7, and the hedge exempted it from every check. A hedge excuses a rounding difference, not an arbitrary one.
The hedge has to be on the page. A sentence that states a bare figure or a bare interval asserts it exactly, and the fact that the true value is close is not a defence. An effect described as running “between 0.30 and 0.50 standard deviations”, about estimates of 0.283 and 0.522, is an erratum, even though both estimates round to the endpoints at one decimal place.

title: Rounding
text:
Differences of printed cells
When the text reports a difference between two printed values, each value was rounded on its own, so the difference can legitimately be off by one unit in the last printed digit. We allowed exactly that, with the tolerance set slightly wider than one unit so that it never sits on a floating-point boundary. Without that margin, a gap of exactly one unit can fail: 0.8 minus 0.7 computes as 0.10000000000000009, which is not at most 0.1.

title: Rounding
text:
The archive’s precision
The deposited code often prints its own output at a fixed precision (a tibble shows three significant digits, a Stata log a few decimals). The archive’s value is compared at the coarser of the page’s precision and the precision the deposited code printed. Any finer comparison manufactures disagreement between two numbers that agree as far as either was ever printed.
Sometimes rounding twice is the deposit’s own convention: a table that rounds to three places and then formats to two prints 0.55 for a rate of 0.5449. The rewrite declines to round twice and computes 0.54, while the archive reproduces the page exactly. We recorded both values and explained in the notes which was which, so that the rewrite’s choice did not read as a failure to reproduce.

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text: Bootstrap intervals, randomization-inference p-values, simulated power, permutation tests, and anything else built on random draws can print a different number on every run. A difference between such a number and the page is not, by itself, evidence of an error. It is not evidence of no error either, and the rule below exists to keep the second mistake from hiding behind the first.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text:
First, confirm that something draws
Before putting a difference down to randomness, we checked that the procedure actually draws at random. A set.seed() call at the top of a script is not evidence of that. One paper set a seed twice and never drew a random number; its results were identical at any seed. An earlier pass had explained a real mismatch in that paper as bootstrap noise from a function that, on inspection, uses the jackknife, which is deterministic. More than once, a difference that looked like noise was a bug.
The check is cheap: run the procedure at two or three very different seeds. If nothing moves, nothing draws, and the difference needs another explanation.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text:
Seeded procedures
When the deposited code sets a seed, the archive check in Stage 1 tries to reproduce the printed value exactly, under the software of the paper’s day. For R, the date that matters most is April 2019: R 3.6.0 changed the default algorithm behind sample(), so code that draws with sample() and was run before then needs RNGkind(sample.kind = "Rounding") to reproduce its own output. We tested the old sampler before concluding that a seeded archive was broken, and it often turned out not to be.
The maintained rewrite keeps the current sampler, because it is the code we would write now. Where the current sampler moves a published number, the ground truth records defect_locus = environment. Neither the paper nor the archive is wrong; the software changed underneath them.
Two practical notes. Setting the sampler inside a script and expecting on.exit() to restore it does not work reliably when scripts are sourced in sequence from run_all.R, so we restored it explicitly and asserted the result. A published number should also be checked under the conditions of the document that printed it: a corrigendum published years after the article may have been computed with different software, or different inputs, from the article it corrects.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text:
Unseeded procedures
When the deposited code sets no seed, the printed value is a single unlabelled draw, and no run can be expected to match it. We reran the procedure across many seeds (a few hundred was usually enough) and asked whether the printed value was consistent with the resulting distribution. Two illustrations:

A chi-squared p-value ran from 0.0005 to 0.004 over 500 replications, and about a quarter of the draws rounded to the printed value. The printed value holds.
The endpoints of a simulated interval were printed as $1.70 and $13.71. Over 200 seeds the endpoints ranged from $1.66 to $1.73 and from $11.79 to $15.19. Both printed values hold.

A printed value far outside any reasonable draw is an erratum. A printed value inside the distribution is not, even when no single run reproduces it.
In the ground truth, such a row leaves match_rewrite empty, since there is no single value to match, and records the verdict in holds. Filling in match_rewrite = TRUE beside a value_rewrite that visibly differs would make the row contradict itself. The same encoding applies whatever the claim type: a pipeline claim whose printed value comes from an unseeded procedure needs it just as much as a descriptive one.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text:
Unseeded figures
The same problem arises in figures, where it is easier to miss. A figure whose layout depends on random draws (a jittered scatter, simulated intervals, labels placed by a stochastic algorithm) can change with every run. In one paper with no seed, 9 of 20 seeds moved at least one published label. The archive runs without error and still cannot reproduce its own figure, even in principle. Where we found this, we measured how much the figure moved at the printed precision and reported it, rather than calling the figure reproduced or not.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: Numbers that come from random draws
text:
In the errata
A value inside the distribution is not an erratum and does not appear in the note. Where such a row carries a locus anyway (a seeded value that the current sampler moves, say, but only within the range over seeds), its disposition is documented_only, with the range as the reason. A value far outside the distribution is an ordinary erratum, and its corrected value is computed from the rewrite in the usual way, with the seed recorded so that the correction itself reproduces.
crumbs: Numbers that come from random draws

title: ground_truth/float_coverage.csv
text:
Rules

The list of floats comes from the article, not from the scripts. An article’s own front matter or numbering says what it contains, and the table is checked against that list, so a float with no script still gets a row.
A figure that prints no numbers is not thereby covered. Its published_numbers is 0, and what it plots is the claim, so plotted and plotted_reproduced carry the check. A figure is never passed just because it prints no numbers.
Some figures cannot be counted. A figure with too many points to count records what the rewrite plots and says so in note; a continuous surface records that it has no discrete points. A diagram that carries no data gets zero counts and a note.
Every count is computed. A typed count once sat a few lines below the code that should have produced it, and claimed eleven covered values where there were three.
The README states each fraction. Computing coverage inside a check that only stops the build leaves a reader with nothing; the report reads this table and prints it.

A paper with no tables or figures writes this table with a header and no rows.
